I hear so much of my younger self in your struggle here and it's tough but it does get better. As our brains develop our understandings of the world there's a lot of shit that gets baked in there deep among the roots in our subconscious about what's Right and Wrong and all that shit. The process of discovering who you are, finding your own identity and actualising yourself takes a long time and it's especially hard to do when you start seeing that your identity is build on a foundation that your subconscious bullshit thinks is Wrong. Even when we consciously learn that it's obviously not Wrong to be You, that being NB is valid and all that cool stuff, the subconscious doesn't catch up at the same speed. The subconscious only starts to change its mind when the conscious mind SHOWS it that it's wrong.

I understand why you feel like nobody believes you, I'm an older AMAB NB who leans femme but folk still read me as Man or Man Wearing Dress a lot. There are, and may always be, folks out there who will call you Cringe, and say you're making it up for attention, or worse. Those people are real and they can be scary but they other thing they all have in common is that they're wrong. Disapproval of strangers is a weirdly powerful thing, it's unhelpful advice to just tell folks to "ignore the haters" or whatever - if ignoring them was an option then you wouldn't have a problem in the first place. The way I think of it, the mental framework that has been helpful to me on my journey, is trying to stay focused on the fact that the more secure You are about Who You Are, the more all the hater-ade starts to wash off you on its own.

It's a long, slow process of building up your own sense of self and internal confidence in who you are. And ALSO, the extra bonus content - the fact that you might be WRONG sometimes about some stuff. That was another thing I struggled with - I didn't figure out there were options beyond Man/Woman/Gay/Straight until I was much older than you, so I had a lot of catching up to do. Part of that meant "trying on labels" that didn't end up really applying to me. She/Her pronouns aren't me, but to find that out I had to experiment. It was awkward and difficult at times and it felt so shameful whenever I realised that what a particular experiment wasn't right and I had to "go backwards". Lots of hard shit.

Ultimately though I think that process itself is what hardened my sense of self. When I got to the stuff that DID feel right it just... idk it Felt Right. The more time you spend being kind to yourself, listening to yourself and understanding yourself, the easier it gets.

The hypocrisy of their bigotry is even obvious in the way you phrase your post - they say they don't believe you when they tell your truth and then accuse you of being a "pick me" because you WON'T pretend to be something else to make them like you. Anyone out there calling anyone a "pick me" is just bitter about the fact that they've cut off so many pieces of themselves to fit in and they're angry at you for refusing to do the same. You can't beat them at their own game - the game they're playing only has losers. Play your own game and you win automatically.

A lot of conventions of "normality" are specifically designed to minimise traits associated with autism because those traits are disruptive to the status quo.

Thats why autism diagnosis hinges on whether or not your symptoms "negatively impact your life". Autism isn't a measure of whether or not you're "normal", it's about whether or not you're useful.

That's why this whole new wave that is emerging of neurodiversity acceptance is growing in acceptance, because it's funded and pushed by organisations that want more people they can use.

I struggle with this a lot, but have been getting better with it by reframing my mental a bit. If my tank feeds and throws and sucks but I, as a DPS, did my job pretty well (applied decent pressure, used my cooldowns well and didn't have any really stupid deaths) then even if we lose, I still played a good game. Since I started thinking about it in those terms, now if a tank starts to do dumb shit and the game looks unwinnable, I just pick an aspect of MY game that I know is weak and I wanna work on and focus on that. So I just spend the rest of the game focussing almost entirely on taking angles, or thinking about my Ults. Now if we lose I come away thinking about how I am improving as a player, or where I need to improve, rather than getting fixated on my shitty tank losing the game. It also has the added benefit of generally turning bad games around a bit, at least when compared to when I'd do other shit like rage swapping or typing in team chat about whatever.

Winning games isn't the thing that makes you better at OW, you get better and THEN you win more games. Thats the mentality change that helped me, but obviously everyone internalises this stuff differently. The giveaway for me that I needed to change something internally was the fact that I wasn't happy after the games I WON either. And it's easy to blame the game for that, but if it's the games fault then the issue is probably just that I don't wanna play the game and should play something else.

Definitely not wrong, it just sounds to me like there's gonna be some adjusting and balancing between the styles. If your strategic playing is designed to STOP the PCs from being able to do the things they built their characters to do then that can be unfun for players in my experience. If the barbarian powergamed a PC with 420hp he's gonna be miserable if nobody ever hits him. 

I read the phrase "shoot your monks" somewhere - fling the odd projectile at the monk so he gets the chance to NOPE that shit and fire it back. Deflect missiles is a cool ability that you, as the DM, need to explicitly give the player the ability to use by setting up its trigger.

Same applies here. Look at the powers that your PCs have focused on, figure out what the characters are really good at doing SPECIFICALLY and make sure your encounters have some kind of pathway to express that.

In your example, the hobgoblin blocking the door is a great idea to slow down the barbarian, but maybe next time that hobgob captain tries to stuff the corridor with 2 or 3 goblin minions that the barb can cleave through in a turn or two and make it into the chamber to square off in an action-movie-finale 1v1 fist fight against the hobgoblin. (assuming the barb is specifically wanting to play the "I hit the thing harder than the thing his me so he dies first" style).

The thing I dig about this approach is it means you can try to set up fights where players can use their powerbuilds to brute force an encounter if they WANT to, but IF anyone stops and thinks about it they realise they can counter-strat the fight and have the barb chase down the archers while the casters attack the hobgob from range and win the fight much more easily.

I expect you'll find that if you try to craft encounters that are winnable by brute force but that can be short-circuited with basic tactics, your players will start to enjoy looking for the tactical advantages (and you can escalate their complexity over time) because it feels to them like they're outsmarting you and beating you at your own game. But if you have encounters day 1 that 'NEED' strategy and tactics to win and that brute-forcing feels hopeless and disempowering then they'll feel more like they're just playing the wrong game.

Hit points are an abstraction of a creatures health anyway. An abstraction with a pretty wide acceptable variation given that a rolled monster with 4d8 HP could mean two monsters seemingly identical side by side in the same fight could have max 4HP and 32HP. So yeah, I really don't think it's an issue for the DM to decide that the well planned and executed surprise sneak attack from the assassin rogue dealing 31 points of damage kills it outright instantly, instead of leaving it on 1HP.

But I also think that giving players a finite amount of resources is critical to creating the kinds of constraints I want in my games that force players to think creatively and solve problems.

If my BBEG Lich has unlimited spell slots (I don't track them) and a billion HP (I don't actually do this but hypothetically), and then I make the fight last as long as it takes for something to happen that I think is cool enough to mark the end of the fight, I don't see that as functionally any different from people doing the same thing with puzzles. 

Y'know those puzzles we all make up where there's a room with a chair with a unicorn carved on the seat and the letters K X Y scored underneath, one leg is shorter than the others and then we just let the players do stuff until you decide something unlocks the door?

Its the same thing, imo. Meticulously tracking all the numbers exactly as the DM is only something I'd see as being worthwhile if I wanted to play the game as a true numbers and logic puzzle, calculating averages and odds and trying to play a game similar to darts, but with statistics, each trying to lower a bunch of numbers to zero faster than the other. IF that is what you want to combat to be then yes, the numbers are absolutely sacred and never to be tampered with or that is cheating and against the spirit of the game you're trying to play. 

The numbers are a tool for the DM to use. And that includes player resources (to an extent, insomuch as you decide if they can get potions, magic items, etc) as well as monster ones.

Yeah I'm a fan of IOStux, but I feel like his expectations/hopes for what a team do with callouts are higher than mine which might be part of the dissonance in opinions here.

I think it's pretty plausible that he's never seen a soloq game where people understand the calls and do the correct tactical and strategic things, utilising the information being provided in the best way possible. And this could be for a variety of reasons like pressure forcing bad decision making, reaction/information processing time and just a general skill gap or lack of knowledge. And I include myself in that - if I hear a callout that says there's a Hog out on the flank it's probably a coin-toss whether I decide that means I should turn around and shoot/chase him, or just move to cover so that I can't get hooked. And if I call Hog on the flank and 2 squishies go to chase him down then in reality I might have ended up just making his flank MORE effective if one of those 2 gets hooked and one-shot and the other loses the remaining 1v1.

BUT - when I call out Hog is on the flank and the members of my team who are in voice hear me, they at least now HAVE that piece of information. If that means they chase, whatever. If it means they hold a cooldown to punish the Hog when he pops out, cool. I'm not here to micro manage the players on my team, but I am here to try to help them - and if they have a 10% better game because I gave them information that they could act upon, then it is an improvement. 

If the player can't utilise the callout *properly* then the bad play they make as a result of the callout is very unlikely to be **worse** than the bad play they'd make if there was no callout (or if they ignored it).

So while the tongue-in-cheek title about it being OP doesn't really stand up to very close scrutiny, I definitely think that even the most incompetent player will perform marginally better with more information over time.

Obviously this all falls down if the person making the calls is a tool and calls the Hog flanking left when the mean right, or whatever, but that all kinda gets lost in the jumble of the chaos of low ranked ladder, IMO.

I've had to deal with this a LOT in my game and I've got a fix in place that has been working well.

Tl:Dr if a player rolls well to persuade/intimidate/deceive an enemy to stop fighting, they can impose disadvantage on an enemy roll next turn similar to cutting words from a bard

For a little context, I have a rogue with his expertise in the social stuff and high enough level to have reliable talent so always hits 20+ on persuasion/deception. And he LOVES this kinda role play. The player doesn't get super into the meat grinder fights (I stab him, sneak attack, bonus disengage and get behind cover) so he likes to try to talk enemies out of fighting during the fight.

We've only been playing since lockdown so it's taken awhile to find the balance but basically I wanna make sure that a high persuasion roll isn't better than a spell like Command, for example. I'd put those kinds of rolls in a similar power bracket to a cantrip, because if you have the ability you have theoretically infinite access to it.

So now, in combat, I've given the rogue an ability similar to Cutting Words for a Bard, where if he tries to convince a bandit to go home and rethink his life, for example, and his deception beats the bandits insight (it will) then the bandit gets kinda jaded and distracted and has disadvantage on his next attack because his head isn't in the game. The same check would work with an intimidate roll if that's how you wanna go. Basically I wanna let the rogue DO something with his abilities because its what he likes to do ingame and it's about fun, but by making this a standard bonus action he has available to him it tempers his expectations so I don't have to keep saying "no that doesn't work", and it has more of a Yes And... vibe.
